n: With both returning groups now safe in Zarahemla, King Mosiah calls the entire population together for a great assembly.
Mormon gives a surprising fact: the descendants of Nephi were a minority in their own land. The people of Zarahemla — descendants of Mulek’s company — outnumbered them.

f.g: A son of Zedekiah, the last king of Judah, who escaped Jerusalem’s fall about 587 BC.

n: Even combined, the Nephites and Mulekites were less than half as many as the Lamanites — a sobering backdrop for the wars that follow in the book of Alma.
The assembly gathers in two groups — Nephites and the people of Zarahemla — showing that the two peoples, though united under one king, still kept distinct identities.
Mosiah reads aloud, and has others read, the record of Zeniff’s colony from the time it left Zarahemla to its return. Much of that record survives in Mosiah 9–22.
He also reads Alma’s account of his group’s journey and sufferings, told in Mosiah 18 and 23–24.
Those who had stayed home in Zarahemla were amazed — for generations they had known little of what happened to Zeniff’s colony.

f.g: Compare the earlier silence: Mosiah 7:1 notes that people in Zarahemla had long wanted to know about those who left.

n: Seeing the freed people before them filled the listeners with great joy.
But remembering those killed by the Lamanites — including Abinadi and many of Limhi’s men — they wept.
Thinking of God’s quick, recent goodness in freeing Alma’s people, they praised him aloud. The account moves through a range of emotions — joy, grief, gratitude, concern.

f.g: “Immediate” here means direct and present — goodness they could see right before them.

n: Finally they felt pain for the Lamanites themselves, whom they still called their brethren. Their concern was for the Lamanites’ souls — a feeling that will soon send Mosiah’s sons on their mission.
The children of Amulon’s priests — born to the Lamanite daughters their fathers had kidnapped — reject their fathers’ wicked ways and choose to be called Nephites instead.

f.w: took upon themselves the name of Nephi
f.g: Taking a new name marks a new identity and loyalty — a theme that culminates in taking the name of Christ.

n: The people of Zarahemla were also counted as Nephites, because the kingship had passed to Nephi’s descendants when Mosiah I arrived and became king over both peoples.

f.w: conferred upon none but those who were descendants of Nephi

n: After his own reading and speaking, Mosiah invites Alma to address the people — a king making room for a prophet.
Alma goes from group to group, preaching repentance and faith in the Lord — the same simple core message he had taught at the waters of Mormon.

f.w: repentance and faith on the Lord

n: Alma urges Limhi’s people to remember that their freedom came from the Lord, not merely from their clever escape plan.

f.g: “Remember” is one of the Book of Mormon’s key words; remembering God’s deliverance keeps people humble.

n: Limhi and his people now ask for baptism. Earlier they had wanted it but had no one with authority to perform it.

f.w: desirous that he might be baptized

n: Alma baptizes them in the same way he had at the waters of Mormon, and they become members of the church because they believed his words.

f.w: after the manner he did his brethren in the waters of Mormon

n: King Mosiah authorizes Alma to establish the church throughout the land and ordain priests and teachers. Civil power supports, but does not run, the church; Alma leads it.
The reason for many congregations was practical: there were too many people for one teacher or one meeting place.

f.w: could not all be governed by one teacher
f.g: Compare Jethro’s counsel to Moses to share the load of leadership.

n: Each local congregation had its own priests and teachers, and all of them taught what Alma had taught them — keeping the doctrine unified.

f.g: Local congregations, much like wards or branches today.

n: Though there were many congregations, they formed one church, the church of God, because they taught the same basic message: repentance and faith in God.
There were seven congregations in the land of Zarahemla. Anyone who wanted to take on the name of Christ could join them.

f.w: take upon them the name of Christ

n: Members were called the people of God. The Lord poured out his Spirit on them, and they prospered — the Book of Mormon’s recurring pattern of blessing for the faithful.
